The Asian giant softshell turtle (*Pelochelys cantorii*), prominently known as Cantor's giant softshell turtle, is one of the most unique and elusive freshwater reptiles on the planet. Native to the slow-moving rivers and estuaries of South and Southeast Asia, this species is immediately recognizable by its bizarre, frog-like face and lack of a hard carapace. Instead of a rigid shell, its back is covered in a smooth, rubbery skin that allows it to seamlessly blend into muddy riverbeds.

These turtles are true giants, capable of growing up to six feet (about two meters) in length and weighing over 100 pounds. As ambush predators, they spend approximately 95 percent of their lives buried beneath the sand or mud. They lie motionless with only their eyes and snout protruding, waiting patiently for passing fish, crustaceans, and mollusks to consume. Remarkably, they only need to surface to take a breath of air a few times a day.

![Adult Cantor's Giant Softshell Turtle](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Pelochelys_cantorii.jpg/640px-Pelochelys_cantorii.jpg)  
*(Photo: Adult Asian Giant Softshell Turtle)*

Unfortunately, the Asian giant softshell turtle is currently classified as Critically Endangered. Decades of rampant habitat destruction, river damming, and illegal poaching for its meat have decimated wild populations. In fact, the species was once thought to be completely extinct in countries like Cambodia, until a small, surviving population was miraculously rediscovered along the Mekong River in 2007. 

![Cantor's Giant Softshell Turtle Hatchling](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Pelochelys_cantorii_hatchling_2.jpg/640px-Pelochelys_cantorii_hatchling_2.jpg)  
*(Photo: Asian Giant Softshell Turtle Hatchling)*

Today, intense, community-based conservation efforts are underway to save the species. Global organizations currently work directly with local residents to protect nesting beaches, collect eggs, and raise hatchlings in specialized facilities before safely releasing them back into the wild. Through these ongoing efforts, conservationists are fighting to bring this magnificent aquatic giant back from the brink of total extinction.

***

### Bibliography

Das, Indraneil. *Turtles of the World*. Johns Hopkins University Press, 2010.

Wildlife Conservation Society. "Cantor's Giant Softshell Turtle." *WCS Cambodia*, cambodia.wcs.org/Wildlife/Cantors-Giant-Softshell-Turtle.aspx. Accessed 24 Oct. 2023.

World Wildlife Fund. "Rare Turtle Discovered in Cambodia's Mekong River." *WWF*, 16 May 2007, wwf.panda.org/wwf_news/?102120/Rare-turtle-discovered-in-Cambodias-Mekong-River. Accessed 24 Oct. 2023.
